title: Accounting Changes
description: Distinguish changes in accounting principle, changes in estimate and changes in reporting entity and apply the appropriate accounting treatment.
html:
Why accounting changes matter

Accounting can change from one reporting period to another for several different reasons.

The accounting treatment depends on what type of change occurred.

Three major categories

  • Change in accounting principle
  • Change in accounting estimate
  • Change in reporting entity

CPA mindset

Solve accounting-change questions in this order:

  1. Identify what changed.
  2. Classify the change.
  3. Determine whether the treatment is retrospective or prospective.
  4. Determine whether prior-period financial statements or beginning equity must be adjusted.

Change in accounting principle

A change in accounting principle occurs when an entity changes from one generally accepted accounting principle to another generally accepted accounting principle.

Example

A company changes its inventory-costing method from FIFO to weighted-average.

This generally represents a change in accounting principle.

General treatment

Changes in accounting principle are generally applied retrospectively when retrospective application is required and practicable.

Retrospective application

Retrospective application generally presents prior periods as though the newly adopted accounting principle had been used in those periods, subject to the applicable guidance.

When necessary, the carrying amounts of assets and liabilities as of the beginning of the earliest period presented are adjusted.

An offsetting adjustment may also be required to the opening balance of retained earnings or another appropriate component of equity.

Simplified example

Assume retrospective application of a new accounting principle requires beginning retained earnings to increase by $24,000.

Beginning retained earnings before adjustment: $400,000

$400,000 + $24,000 = $424,000 adjusted beginning retained earnings

CPA trap

Retrospective application does not mean putting the entire effect of the change into current-period net income.

Change in accounting estimate

Estimates are necessary because some amounts cannot be known with certainty when financial statements are prepared.

New information or new experience may cause management to revise an estimate.

Examples

  • Useful life of depreciable equipment
  • Residual value
  • Expected credit losses
  • Certain warranty obligations
  • Other estimates affected by updated information

General treatment

Changes in accounting estimates are generally accounted for prospectively.

Prior-period financial statements are not revised merely because an estimate changed based on new information.

Prospective treatment

Prospective treatment affects the current period and, when applicable, future periods.

Depreciation estimate example

Equipment originally cost: $120,000

Accumulated depreciation at the date of the estimate change: $48,000

Revised residual value: $12,000

Revised remaining useful life: 5 years

Step 1 — Determine carrying amount

$120,000 − $48,000 = $72,000

Step 2 — Determine remaining depreciable amount

$72,000 − $12,000 = $60,000

Step 3 — Calculate revised annual depreciation

$60,000 ÷ 5 = $12,000 per year

Previously recognized depreciation is not rewritten merely because the estimate changed.

Change in estimate effected by a change in accounting principle

Sometimes separating a change in principle from a change in estimate is difficult because the new accounting method is adopted as a consequence of a change in estimate.

Such a change is treated as a change in accounting estimate and therefore generally accounted for prospectively.

Classic CPA example

A change in depreciation method is generally treated as a change in estimate effected by a change in accounting principle.

Therefore, it is generally applied prospectively.

CPA trap

Seeing the word "method" does not automatically mean retrospective treatment.

A change in depreciation method is the major exception you should recognize.

Change in reporting entity

A change in reporting entity occurs when financial statements are presented for an entity that is different from the entity represented in previously issued financial statements.

Examples can include

  • Changing the subsidiaries included in consolidated financial statements in a manner constituting a change in reporting entity
  • Changing the companies included in combined financial statements

General treatment

Changes in reporting entity are generally applied retrospectively to financial statements of prior periods presented.

Principle vs estimate

Accounting Principle

Change from one acceptable accounting principle to another.

Generally retrospective.

Accounting Estimate

Revision resulting from new information or experience.

Generally prospective.

Accounting change versus error

An accounting change is not the same thing as correcting an accounting error.

A legitimate revision of an estimate caused by new information is not an error merely because the old estimate turned out to be different from the final result.

Estimate change

A machine was originally expected to last ten years, but new information indicates that it will now last only eight years.

Assuming the original estimate was reasonable when made, this is generally a change in estimate rather than an error.

Error

A company discovers that a prior-year mathematical calculation was simply wrong.

That is an error, not a change in estimate.

Error corrections are covered in Lesson 8.

Quick classification framework

FIFO → Weighted-Average Principle
Revised Useful Life Estimate
Revised Residual Value Estimate
Change in Depreciation Method Estimate effected by Principle Change
Change in Reporting Entity Reporting Entity
Prior Mathematical Mistake Error

Worked CPA-style example

On January 1, a company determines that equipment's remaining useful life should change from six years to four years because of newly available information.

Carrying amount on January 1: $92,000

Revised residual value: $12,000

Step 1 — Classify the change

Revised useful life based on new information is a change in estimate.

Step 2 — Determine treatment

Apply the change prospectively.

Step 3 — Calculate revised depreciation

($92,000 − $12,000) ÷ 4 = $20,000 per year

Prior-period depreciation is not restated.

What you should know after this lesson

  • Distinguish a change in principle from a change in estimate.
  • Know that changes in principle are generally retrospective.
  • Know that changes in estimates are generally prospective.
  • Recognize a change in depreciation method as a change in estimate effected by a change in principle.
  • Understand the treatment of a change in reporting entity.
  • Distinguish legitimate accounting changes from errors.
  • Recalculate depreciation correctly after an estimate change.

quiz.prompt: A company changes the estimated remaining useful life of equipment because new information indicates that the asset will be productive for longer than previously expected. How should the change generally be accounted for?

choices.text: Prospectively as a change in accounting estimate
Retrospectively by restating all prior financial statements
Directly through beginning additional paid-in capital

quiz.explanation: A revision of useful life based on new information is a change in accounting estimate. Changes in estimates are generally accounted for prospectively in the period of change and future periods when affected.

objectives: Explain accounting changes and its underlying principles.
Apply the topic to a financial-reporting scenario.
Evaluate common errors and their financial-statement effects.
